question: How does the run budget estimate how many tokens a run has spent, given that the AI provider doesn't report usage?
answer: It estimates from output length: estimateTokens(text) = ceil(len/4) over the response text; exact usage is deferred and the estimate is an accepted risk.
core: Estimates from output length: ceil(text length / 4).
evidence: The AIProvider returns only text ( claude.ts:71,131 ) — no usage to read. Decision estimateTokens(text) = ceil(len/4) ;
note: Single design decision; 'len/4' appears nowhere else in specs/. The parent #decisions section also contains it, but D-001 is the smallest element.

question: How does spectastic add trailers to its automatic commits: does it assemble the commit-message footer itself?
answer: No. run.commit appends one git commit --trailer flag per trailer entry, so git owns RFC-correctness and dedup; this needs git >= 2.32, with interpret-trailers as the fallback.
core: No; it passes one git --trailer flag per trailer and lets git build the footer.
evidence: Decision run.commit(subject, trailers) appends one --trailer flag per entry. No manual footer assembly, no second process. Consequences + Git owns RFC-correctness + dedup.
note: Tests a design decision. tasks.html#T-013 and #T-902 mention --trailer and git >= 2.32 in passing but not the 'no manual footer' point.

question: What made the lines of a wrapped heading overlap when the heading contained inline code?
answer: The h1 line-height of 1.05 was too tight, and inline code's padding, border and 0.9em size made a ~73px box inside a 57px line box; the fix raised h1 line-height to 1.14 and flattened code inside headings.
core: The h1 line-height (1.05) was too tight for inline code's padded, bordered box.
evidence: root cause was the tight heading line-height:1.05 plus inline code's padding/border/0.9em box exceeding the line box (≈73px vs 57px); fixed in base CSS by loosening h1 line-height to 1.14
note: Triage-log card. '1.05' occurs only in this card. Element is 223 words, near the upper size limit.

question: In the VS Code extension's canvas, why was the hover card cut off for nodes near the edge of the panel?
answer: The card was appended inside the canvas surface, which the scroll container clips with overflow:auto. The fix renders it on document.body with position:fixed, viewport clamping and flip-above.
core: The card rendered inside the scroll container, which clipped it (overflow:auto).
evidence: root cause was implementation drift — the card was appended inside the canvas surface, which the scroll container clips with overflow:auto ; fixed by rendering it on <body> with position:fixed , viewport clamping, and flip-above;
note: Triage-log card. 'position:fixed' appears only in this card within 020.

question: Why did the npm publish of v0.1.0-pre.28 fail?
answer: It was a credential failure, not a code one: the npm step returned 404 Not Found on the PUT for @spectastic/render, which points to NPM_TOKEN expiring, rotating or losing scope. The fix moved publishing to OIDC trusted publishing.
core: An npm credential failure (404 on publish: token expired or lost scope), not a code failure.
evidence: The v0.1.0-pre.28 publish failed twice at the npm step with 404 Not Found - PUT …/@spectastic%2frender — a credential failure, not a code one (every gate passed).
note: Archived (applied) proposal. tasks.html#T-1405 only says to re-run the tag. Element is 184 words.

question: Spectastic plans to point configuration files at a version-pinned copy of its config schema on the package registry's CDN. At the pinned release, can that copy actually be fetched yet?
answer: No. Fetching it at the pinned version returns 404 because the currently published version predates the schema file, so the check is to be repeated at the next release.
core: No; it returns 404 because the published version predates the schema file.
grading: Scored against the archive at v0.1.0-pre.28, not today's npm: @spectastic/schema has since been published, which is a later fact.
evidence: Deliberately unticked: it returns 404 today, because the currently-published version predates the schema file. Repeat at the next release
note: Tasks file. design.html#risks names the 404 as a risk, but only T-301 states the current status. The archive contradicts itself: 087 design.html#grounding (4 Aug) says the CDN address returned HTTP 200 at 0.1.0-pre.23, in the same commit as T-301's 404; T-301's later note (18 Aug) agrees with the 404, so the reference answer stands.

question: When the kernel was extracted, what benchmark baseline was full-project validation expected to stay within 20% of?
answer: The validate-full-project p50 should stay within ±20% of 175 ms on an M1 dev machine and 295 ms on ubuntu-latest CI.
core: 175 ms on an M1 dev machine and 295 ms on ubuntu-latest CI (validate-full-project p50).
evidence: The validate-full-project bench scenario's p50 SHOULD stay within ±20% of today's baseline (175 ms on M1 dev; 295 ms on ubuntu-latest CI).
note: Spec NFR. 006 tasks.html repeats the 295 ms CI figure but not the 175 ms M1 figure. Element is 35 words.

question: In the change-risk verification run, what result did a diff with a staged binary plus a CI workflow edit produce?
answer: Two findings, a 55/100 amber score and the disclaimer, with exit code 0.
core: Two findings, a 55/100 amber score and the disclaimer (exit 0).
evidence: (1) a staged binary + CI-workflow edit prints two findings, a 55/100 amber score, and the disclaimer, exit 0;
note: Verify file, Run/Demo block. '55/100' appears only here. spec.html#SC-001 describes the same fixture but gives no number.

question: Why does triage fan-out use a hand-rolled concurrency pool instead of the p-map library?
answer: p-map is only a dev/CI transitive dependency, and promoting it would add a real runtime dependency to the published package. The owner kept @spectastic/core dependency-minimal, so a ~30-line mapPool copies p-map's input-order and concurrency-cap semantics.
core: To avoid adding p-map as a runtime dependency of the published core package.
evidence: p-map@7.0.4 is the obvious library but is only a dev/CI transitive via @secretlint/node ( pnpm-lock.yaml:2597 ) — promoting it adds a real runtime dep to the published package.
note: Design decision; 'p-map' occurs only in this file. spec.html#FR-007 (default cap 8) is related but does not give the reason.

question: Why does a design page bake in a duplicate of the API definition's text instead of pulling that file in live while someone is viewing it?
answer: The artifact's Content-Security-Policy (default-src 'none', no connect-src) blocks a runtime fetch, and an iframe would be flagged by the no-executable-content rule, so the contract text is copied in at generate time and drift is guarded separately.
core: The page's Content-Security-Policy forbids fetching at view time, so the text is copied in when the page is generated.
evidence: templates/design.html:6 sets default-src 'none' with no connect-src , so a runtime fetch is blocked by policy; <iframe> is separately flagged by the no-executable-content rule.
note: Paraphrase of 'materialise, never transclude'. The #questions sections in spec and design name the choice but not the reason.

question: If someone tweaks a file that came in from a design tool and later brings in a fresh version from that tool, are their tweaks kept?
answer: Yes, manual changes survive a re-import, except on fields whose source of truth is the export; those fields are re-derived on every import.
core: Yes, except fields whose source of truth is the export, which are re-derived.
evidence: A hand edit to landed material MUST survive a re-import, except where the field has a source of truth in the export.
note: The answer is in two places (requirement and the design decision that implements it). Evidence is taken from FR-009.

question: How does the prose theme make sure its fade-in-on-scroll effect can never leave text invisible if the page's code fails to load or errors out?
answer: The stylesheet never hides anything. The script marks the document as reveal-capable when it runs, and only then does the hidden state exist, so a failure degrades to plain visible content.
core: The reveal is a progressive enhancement: nothing is hidden unless the script has run, so a failure leaves text visible.
evidence: The stylesheet never hides a block. The script marks the document as reveal-capable when it runs, and only then does the unrevealed state exist.
note: Asks for the mechanism. spec.html#NFR-002 states the requirement (readable with JavaScript off) but not how it is met.

question: Once a project's knowledge base outgrows simple lookup, which search upgrades should be layered on, in what sequence, and how much does each one help?
answer: Contextual embeddings, then contextual BM25, then reranking, in that order. They cut retrieval failures by roughly a third, a half and two-thirds respectively.
core: Contextual embeddings, then contextual BM25, then reranking; each cuts retrieval failures further (about a third, a half, two-thirds).
evidence: retrieval SHOULD follow the known ladder — contextual embeddings, then contextual BM25, then reranking — in that order. Rationale The ladder is characterised: the three stages cut retrieval failures by roughly a third, a half, and two-thirds respectively.
note: 051 spec.html#requirements (1,173 words) mentions 'embeddings + BM25 + reranking' as out of scope, but not as an ordered ladder and without the failure-reduction figures.

question: Will validation stop me from checking in a reference book whose terms forbid sharing it?
answer: No. A redistribution-restricted document raises a corpus-license finding at warning severity, not an error, because committing it is the project's call; the rule only makes the fact visible.
core: No; it raises a warning, not an error.
evidence: A warning, not an error: whether to commit restricted material is a project's call to make with the fact in front of it. The rule's job is to make the fact unavoidable, not to block the decision.
note: design.html#D-001 also says 'Warning severity (FR-002)' but gives no rationale, so FR-002 is the full answer.

question: Is it acceptable for a success criterion to require that something never happens, or always happens, without giving any reasoning?
answer: No. A criterion asserting a threshold of 0 or 100% (or two equal thresholds) must carry a stated justification, because a bare absolute is often an unfalsifiable reflex.
core: No; a 0 or 100% threshold needs a stated justification.
evidence: A criterion asserting a threshold of 0 or 100%, or two equal thresholds, MUST carry a stated justification.
note: Paraphrases 'threshold of 0 or 100%' as 'never/always'. tasks.html#T-117 mentions a 'bare zero' fixture but not the rule.

question: If the one-step visual flow is given a path to a design handoff that it can't open, how far does it get before giving up?
answer: It refuses straight away, before any model call or any file write, and names the path it could not read.
core: It refuses immediately, before any model call or file write, naming the path it couldn't read.
evidence: Before making any model call and before writing any file, the invocation MUST refuse when the named export cannot be read, and MUST state which path it could not read.
note: Related posture in 106 FR-005 (refuse before executing any artboard) is a different, later stage.

question: What performance problem pushed the project to break its flagship specification document into several smaller ones?
answer: At 118 KB the meta-spec took about 140 ms to validate on CI (about 28 ms locally) against a 100 ms per-file budget, so the project failed its own performance requirement.
core: The meta-spec had grown too big to validate within the project's own per-file time budget on CI.
evidence: At 118 KB the meta-spec takes about 28 ms to validate on a developer machine and roughly 140 ms on a continuous-integration runner, against a budget of 100 ms per file
note: Archived (applied) proposal. '118 KB' and '140 ms' appear only here. Element is 190 words.

question: Why did the auto-generated verification pages scroll sideways on a narrow phone screen, and how was it fixed?
answer: renderVerifyHtml emitted the trace and observables tables with no scroll container. Both tables are now wrapped in an overflow-x:auto container where they are emitted.
core: The tables had no horizontal scroll container; they are now wrapped in one (overflow-x:auto).
evidence: root cause was renderVerifyHtml emitting the trace and observables tables with no scroll container; fixed by wrapping them at the point of emission;
note: Triage-log card. Avoids 'overflow', 'unwrapped tables' and '390 px'.

question: In a generated course, learners had nowhere to type their own explanation of an idea. What was wrong, and what changed?
answer: The implementation rendered the teach-back prompt as static prose with no input. It now renders a textarea under the prompt, labelled as not saved, because course content isn't persisted.
core: The prompt had no input; an (unsaved) textarea was added under it.
evidence: root cause was the implementation rendering the prompt as static prose with no input; fixed by adding a non-persisted <textarea> ;
note: Triage-log card. Avoids 'teach-back', 'affordance' and 'textarea'.

question: What does FR-001 of spec 040, the run budget, require of the BudgetTracker?
answer: It must accumulate the run's estimated output-token spend and expose a phase: normal below 80% of the ceiling, degrade at >=80%, halt at >=100% (always normal when there is no ceiling).
core: Accumulate estimated output-token spend and report a phase: normal below 80%, degrade at 80%, halt at 100% of the ceiling.
evidence: A BudgetTracker MUST accumulate the run's estimated output-token spend and expose its phase : normal below 80% of the ceiling, degrade at ≥ 80%, halt at ≥ 100%.
note: Identifier lookup; FR-001 exists in ~120 files, so the spec number/name must disambiguate. Thresholds 80%/100% are also common elsewhere (REQ-FORMAT-004 amber).

question: What does NFR-001 in spec 045, artifact security, require?
answer: FR-001 and FR-002 must be deterministic and must not break the rendering or interactivity of any existing spec-family artifact type, verified by opening representative artifacts in a browser.
core: The two requirements it covers (FR-001 and FR-002, named or described) must be deterministic and must not break rendering or interactivity of existing artifact types.
grading: An answer may describe what FR-001 and FR-002 require instead of naming them.
evidence: FR-001 and FR-002 MUST be deterministic and MUST NOT break the rendering or interactivity of any existing spec-family artifact type
note: Identifier lookup on NFR-001 (~117 occurrences corpus-wide). The element refers to FR-001/FR-002 without restating them; Brian may want the answer to say what those are.

question: What does success criterion SC-002 of spec 119, decision resource scope, measure?
answer: That a reviewer in a consuming service is flagged, at the decision's declared posture, when their change touches a store owned elsewhere, in both the direct-write and own-adapter cases: 2 of 2 non-owner fixture scenarios (C and D) must flag.
core: That a change touching a store owned elsewhere is flagged for a non-owner, in both the direct-write and own-adapter cases (2 of 2 scenarios).
evidence: A reviewer in a consuming service is flagged, at the decision's declared posture, when their change touches a store owned elsewhere — in both the direct-write and the well-layered-own-adapter case: 2 of 2 non-owner fixture scenarios flag
note: Identifier lookup on an SC (a <spec-criterion>, ~116 SC-002s corpus-wide); many neighbouring guardrail specs (112-120) have near-identical SC-002 vocabulary.

question: In the design for spec 026, git strategy, what does decision D-002 settle about where configuration lives?
answer: Config lives in a root spectastic.json with a git section ({"git": {"auto": "off"}}); an absent file or key falls back to defaults (auto=off), chosen over a hidden .spectastic/ directory.
core: In a root spectastic.json (git section), with defaults when the file or key is absent.
evidence: Read a root spectastic.json with a git section ( { "git": { "auto": "off" } } ); absent file or key → defaults ( auto=off ).
note: Identifier lookup on a decision (D-002 in ~112 design files). spectastic.json is mentioned in 14 other spec.html files (e.g. 033, 044, 067), plausible distractors.

question: What is task T-100 in the task list for spec 065, corpus PDF convert?
answer: Write a failing test that the default convert path (MarkItDown), with the stub runner and fixture shim, reaches the same terminal pack state as an equivalent adaptCorpus call, in packages/corpus/test/knowledge.convert.test.ts.
core: A failing test that the default MarkItDown convert path reaches the same pack state as adaptCorpus.
evidence: Write failing test: default convert files a doc — with the stub runner + fixture shim, the default (MarkItDown) path reaches the same terminal pack state as an equivalent adaptCorpus call.
note: Identifier lookup on a task; T-100 appears in ~118 tasks files, nearly all of them 'write failing test' tasks, so naive search is easily confused.

question: What does FR-003 of spec 103, content budgets, say about checking a budget?
answer: A budget must be treated as a design constraint and must not be checked against any running text, because the real copy lives in systems the vocabulary cannot see.
core: A budget is a design constraint and must not be checked against running text.
evidence: A budget MUST be treated as a design constraint and MUST NOT be checked against any running text.
note: Identifier lookup; FR-003 is in ~122 files. 'Budget' also collides with spec 040 (run budget) and the spec-budget words gauge.

question: What is decision D-001 in the design for spec 078, the federated resource URI?
answer: The corpus kind joins the existing shared composer: extend ResourceKind with 'corpus', add a thin named wrapper, and add an optional edition parameter emitted as ?edition= before any fragment.
core: Add a corpus kind to the existing shared resource-URI composer, with an optional edition parameter.
evidence: Extend ResourceKind with 'corpus' and add a thin named wrapper beside the existing spec and contract wrappers. Add an optional edition parameter to the shared composer, emitted as ?edition= before any fragment.
note: Identifier lookup on D-001 (~112 design files). Resource-URI coordinates are discussed in many specs (067, 076, 095, 112), all plausible distractors.

question: What is success criterion SC-001 of spec 100, screen flows?
answer: For a feature declaring a journey, a reader can state the order of its screens and the failure branch of each step from the declaration alone, opening 0 other files.
core: A reader can tell the screen order and each step's failure branch from the declaration alone, opening no other file.
evidence: For a feature declaring a journey, a reader can state the order of its screens and the failure branch of each step from the declaration alone, opening 0 other files.
note: Identifier lookup on SC-001 (~126 occurrences, the most common SC id). Element is exactly 30 words, at the low end of the preferred range.

question: Which success criteria in spec 109, the prose theme, validate FR-008 (the receding sticky header)?
answer: Two: SC-003 (keyboard readers reach every control the receding header carries, 100%) and SC-001 (reviewers read a long artifact end to end in one sitting); both list FR-008 in their validates attribute.
core: SC-003 and SC-001.
evidence: Readers navigating by keyboard reach every control the receding header carries — share reachable 100% (target 100%), from no established baseline.
note: Follows <spec-criterion validates=...>: SC-001 validates FR-002..FR-005,FR-008,FR-009; SC-003 validates FR-008. The link lives only in an attribute, so body-text chunks don't contain 'FR-008' in either criterion.

question: Which requirements does success criterion SC-002 of spec 110, visual one-step, validate, and what do they demand?
answer: FR-003 and NFR-001: before any model call or file write, the invocation must refuse when the named export cannot be read and name the path; a refusing run makes 0 model calls and writes 0 files.
core: FR-003 and NFR-001: refuse before any model call or write when the export can't be read, naming the path; 0 model calls, 0 files written.
evidence: Before making any model call and before writing any file, the invocation MUST refuse when the named export cannot be read, and MUST state which path it could not read.
note: Follows SC-002's validates="FR-003,NFR-001" to the far end. SC-002 itself (mistyped export path loses nothing) is the near end and is not listed as expected; add it if Brian wants both ends.

question: Spec 058's corpus-license rule reads a license field that 058 says it does not own. Which spec defines that field, and what else goes in that frontmatter?
answer: 051-knowledge-corpus (FR-003): every corpus document carries provenance frontmatter of origin/origin-url, edition, license, converter, a content hash and a status.
core: 051-knowledge-corpus: provenance frontmatter with origin, edition, license, converter, content hash and status. Citing FR-003 is preferred but not required.
grading: The question asks for the spec, not the requirement; an answer without FR-003 is correct.
evidence: Every corpus document MUST carry provenance frontmatter: origin / origin-url , edition , license , converter , a content hash, and a status (e.g. illustrative-excerpt vs authoritative).
note: Follows defer-to="051-knowledge-corpus" on 058's out-of-scope item 'The license provenance field this rule reads.' The near end is the whole 247-word requirements section (no smaller id holds the out-of-scope list).

question: Spec 055 (corpus in review) leaves injecting the corpus into the authoring verbs out of scope. Which spec handles that, and what does it require?
answer: 054-corpus-in-prompt: when a corpus is present, core must inject its index and a grounding directive into every AI-verb prompt, using the same fenced mechanism that injects the principles.
core: 054-corpus-in-prompt: inject the corpus index and a grounding directive into every AI-verb prompt.
evidence: When a corpus is present, core MUST inject its index and a grounding directive into every AI-verb prompt, via the same fenced mechanism that already injects the principles.
note: Follows defer-to="054-corpus-in-prompt" on 055's out-of-scope list. Near end is 055's 279-word requirements section (slightly over the preferred size; no smaller id).

question: Spec 023's design dropped its decision on generating restore tasks after an exploration graduates. Which slice took that over, and how is restore invoked now?
answer: It moved to the sibling slice TBD-explore-restore, now 024-explore-restore, where restore is a mode of /spectastic.tasks: /spectastic.tasks <id> --restore, or an announced prompt when a graduated marker is present.
core: 024-explore-restore; restore is now a mode of /spectastic.tasks (--restore).
evidence: US2 (restore-scaffold) was split to the sibling slice TBD-explore-restore when 023's budget went red (the spec's INVEST·Small trigger).
note: Follows a superseded decision to its new owner. D-006 names the placeholder TBD-explore-restore; that it became 024 is stated in 024's tasks.html ('024 now exists'), not in D-006. Brian should check he accepts that hop.

question: Which spec superseded 001-cli, and what did it require happen to the old Python CLI?
answer: 003-init-node-port: at its apply, scripts/spectastic and scripts/test_spectastic.py were removed and 001-cli's status flipped to superseded with a forward link to 003; 001 stays as historical record.
core: 003-init-node-port; the Python CLI scripts were removed and 001-cli was marked superseded.
evidence: the Python script scripts/spectastic and its test file scripts/test_spectastic.py MUST be removed from the repository, and spec 001-cli 's <spec-status> MUST flip to superseded with a forward link to this spec.
note: Supersession link. The forward link in 001-cli sits in a header <spec-note> with no id, so only the far end (003 FR-010) is addressable.

question: Spec 076 emits a change notification when a contract is promoted. Which spec provides that promotion hook, and where does promotion actually run?
answer: 071-contract-promotion (its US1 promotion hook); per 071's D-002, promotion runs inside applyCommand, immediately before the existing proposal-archive step, with no new verb. At the pinned tag that is still the design, though an open triage finding (071 triage-log T-001, 13 Aug 2026) records that it leaves a first design, which has no change proposal, with no way to promote, and proposes giving promotion an entry point of its own.
core: 071-contract-promotion; promotion runs inside apply, just before the proposal is archived.
grading: Core unchanged. Mentioning the open T-001 finding is a bonus, not required. Saying promotion already has its own entry point is wrong at the pinned tag: T-001's 'fixed by' line describes the proposed fix, and 071's spec and D-002 are unchanged.
evidence: 071 US1 → US2 (the promotion hook the notification fires from)
note: Dependency link across specs. 076's design.html also cites 071 D-002 in its grounding table ('071 is a hard prerequisite'), but that section is 301 words, so the 48-word tasks dependencies section is used as the near end.

question: How does spec 004's npm publish workflow derive the dist-tag, and what implements that logic?
answer: A tested Node script, scripts/derive-dist-tag.mjs: a pure deriveDistTags(version, publishedVersions) plus one network function, keyed on whether a stable release exists, and failing rather than guessing when registry state is unknown.
core: A tested Node script (scripts/derive-dist-tag.mjs) that derives the tag from whether a stable release exists.
evidence: move the derivation into scripts/derive-dist-tag.mjs , splitting a pure deriveDistTags(version, publishedVersions) from the one function that touches the network.
note: Stale D-005 (superseded by D-006): an inline bash conditional, hyphen in version -> next, else latest. Check: D-006's 'extra tags via npm dist-tag add' has since been overtaken by FR-006 (OIDC, publish straight to latest pre-stable), and the risks table still cites D-005's bash conditional.

question: How quickly must spectastic init complete in an empty directory?
answer: Under 500 ms p95 on a modern laptop (Apple M-series or comparable); the work is pure filesystem with no network.
core: Under 500 ms p95.
evidence: Init MUST complete in under 500 ms p95 on a modern laptop (Apple M-series or comparable) in an empty directory.
note: Stale: superseded 001-cli (the Python CLI) set under 2 seconds wall-clock (NFR-001) / under 2 seconds at p95 (SC-003, 13 words). 001's whole spec is superseded by 003.

question: What are the eight lifecycle slash commands spectastic must ship?
answer: /spectastic.principles, .spec, .design, .tasks, .implement, .propose, .apply and .triage.
core: principles, spec, design, tasks, implement, propose, apply and triage.
grading: Extended opt-in verbs (explain, explore, ...) are never required; mentioning them is neither credit nor penalty.
evidence: Spectastic MUST ship eight Claude Code slash commands across the lifecycle — /spectastic.principles , /spectastic.spec , /spectastic.design , /spectastic.tasks , /spectastic.implement , /spectastic.propose , /spectastic.apply , /spectastic.triage
note: Stale: the withdrawn proposal 2026-06-13-implement-to-build carries a REQ-TOOL-001 delta listing /spectastic.build instead of /spectastic.implement. REQ-TOOL-001 now lives in 090 (moved out of the 000 meta-spec).

question: In spec 094, the visual sidecar convention, which operation must stat only the declared paths, and what are its limits?
answer: Path resolution: at most 1 filesystem call per declaration and 0 directory walks, so a project with many specs pays a cost linear in declarations rather than files.
core: Path resolution: at most 1 filesystem call per declaration and 0 directory walks.
evidence: Path resolution MUST stat only the declared paths: at most 1 filesystem call per declaration, and at most 0 directory walks
note: Stale: withdrawn 'bind the checks' widened the subject to 'Every check' and named view materialisation as an exception bounded by the owning spec. A second withdrawn sibling (bound-what-it-binds) kept 'path resolution' but reworded the purpose and pointed to 099 NFR-003; not listed as stale because its answer to this question is the same.

question: In spec 099, the visual embedded view, what must happen when a materialised view no longer matches what it projects, and what is it compared against?
answer: It must be reported, comparing the view against the files it projects as they currently are, not against a stored digest.
core: It must be reported, comparing against the projected files as they are now.
evidence: A view that no longer matches the files it projects MUST be reported, compared against those files as they are rather than a stored digest.
note: Stale: withdrawn 'absence is not drift' narrowed drift to the screens a view projects and said render presence must never count as drift. It was withdrawn because its premise was false: nothing resolves a render's src, per 099's changelog.

question: How is an individual declared screen addressed by a resource coordinate in spectastic?
answer: By a resource coordinate of its own kind, qualified by the owning spec; each screen must declare the name it is addressed by, and two screens in one spec resolving to the same name are an error.
core: By a screen resource coordinate of its own kind, qualified by the owning spec, using the name the screen declares.
evidence: A declared screen MUST be addressable by a resource coordinate of its own kind, qualified by the spec that owns it; a screen MUST declare the name it is addressed by
note: Stale (archived, later replaced): 2026-08-14-use-the-anchor made a screen an anchor in its spec's URI (spectastic://<project>/spec/<spec-id>#<anchor>); 2026-08-13-address-a-screen used 'the kind the project already uses'. Current element is 326 words.

question: How does the verify view (spec 021) decide which tasks are test tasks when tracing success criteria, and what happens if a story phase has no Tests subsection?
answer: The primary signal is a task under the story's 'Tests (write & fail first)' subsection; when a phase has no Tests subsection, it falls back to a file-path test pattern (.test. / .spec.).
core: Tasks under the story's Tests subsection; otherwise a .test./.spec. file-path pattern.
evidence: When a story phase declares no Tests subsection, the aggregation MUST fall back to identifying test tasks by file path — a <spec-task> whose declared path matches a test-file pattern ( .test. / .spec. ).
note: Stale (archived, later amended by 2026-07-09-verify-trace-path-fallback): the 2026-06-27 trace-by-tests-section wording used structural position only, independent of file path, with no fallback. Current element is exactly 250 words.

question: Is there a JetBrains plugin (IntelliJ or WebStorm) for spectastic's lifecycle canvas, like the VS Code extension?
answer: Not covered in specs/.
core: Declines: not covered.
note: Adjacent to 020-vscode-extension. grep -i: jetbrains, intellij, webstorm, 'plugin for' (the one hit is an unrelated 'diffing plugin for a design system') all give 0 relevant hits.

answer: Not covered in specs/.
core: Declines: not covered.
note: grep -i: jira, atlassian, '\btickets?\b', 'issue tracker', 'GitHub Issues' all give 0 hits. 'Linear' appears only as the inspiration for the inbox, not as an integration.

question: Which compliance frameworks, such as SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR or ISO 27001, does the enterprise profile map its controls to?

question: What does running spectastic's init with the tools option set up in a project, and what happens if the project already has a git hook of its own?
answer: It installs spectastic's guarantee layer, in two halves. First, a git pre-commit hook that runs spectastic validate over the whole artifact set and rejects the commit on any error (and on an open question in an Accepted spec). Second, the Claude Code command adapters, installed so they cannot drift from their commands/*.md source (generated or linked, not copied once). An existing pre-commit hook is preserved: the spectastic gate is chained alongside it and the old hook is never overwritten. The command is explicit and idempotent, and outside a git repository it installs only the adapters, with a warning.
core: a pre-commit hook that runs validate and blocks a commit on errors; Claude Code command adapters that cannot drift from their source; an existing hook is kept and chained, not overwritten
evidence: init --tools MUST install a git pre-commit hook that runs spectastic validate over the project's whole artifact set on each commit.
note: Replaces G-005 at Brian's request (a question on what init --tools does, rather than whether it wires in enforce). Same stratum as G-005 (single-fact), so the single-fact count stays at 10 if kept. Three expected elements in one spec: all@4 needs three of the four slots. Checked that no later spec changes what --tools installs: 003 FR-002 says --tools adds a hook and a managed-adapter stamp; 041 keeps --profile independent of --tools; 042 FR-005 (wire in enforce) is SHOULD and deferred (the old G-005). Shares the flag name and 'hook' with FR-002/FR-006 because the question cannot avoid naming the command.

question: Releases normally go out through CI. Why would spectastic also let a maintainer publish straight from their own laptop, and what do they give up by doing it that way?
answer: Because CI is not always available: GitHub Actions can be down, the OIDC issuer can be rate-limiting, or the maintainer may need to ship a hotfix from a network where the CI secrets are unreachable. CI stays the default because it bundles every release gate into one trigger, but the local fallback makes that day non-existential: the maintainer authenticates to npm directly and runs pnpm publish -r. The price is the provenance badge, which only the CI path provides.
core: CI is not always available (Actions down, OIDC issuer rate-limiting, secrets unreachable for an urgent hotfix); the cost is losing the provenance badge / attestation
evidence: CI is not available 100% of the time.

question: Why did spectastic add a command that explains a finished spec to whoever is reading it, instead of leaving them to ask a general-purpose chatbot?
answer: A junior engineer or product reviewer who lands on a finished spec had no in-tool way to understand it, so they left for a chat window, where any explanation is ungrounded and free to invent APIs and requirements that don't exist. explain was added as an opt-in extended verb so the explanation stays grounded in the actual spec, without bloating the default command surface; it was built coach-first, with a persistent course once grounding was proven.

question: Spectastic makes you pin down exactly what you want before anything gets written. What made it add a way to hack on something first and work out what you want as you go?
answer: That up-front rigor forfeits the one thing ordinary AI coding does well: building something, running it, and letting the attempt show you what you actually wanted. Sometimes you don't know what to build until you've tried, and the existing fast path (the just-do inbox card) only helps with changes you already understand. Spectastic rejects the choice between vibe-coding and forbidding prototypes: an exploratory build can be the best source for a good spec if it is graduated into one rather than shipped, and it is kept in quarantine so nothing loose reaches production.
core: sometimes you don't know what to build until you've tried; building to learn is what the rigour gives up; the prototype feeds a spec (graduated, not shipped) and is quarantined so nothing reaches production
evidence: Sometimes you don't know what to build until you've tried.

question: What problem led spectastic to add checks that the same spec number or requirement id isn't handed out twice?
answer: Spectastic keeps readable, sequential directory numbers, and allocating the next one is not atomic, so two developers on two branches can both mint the same number. The project chose to catch that loudly at merge time in CI rather than give up the readable ids, but nothing flagged two directories sharing a number. A second gap was a spec-local id such as FR-001 declared twice within one file, which a re-entry edit can silently open. The slice adds two pure validation rules for these, as the foundation later git-strategy work assumes.
core: two developers on separate branches can both mint the same spec number, and nothing flagged it; a spec-local id declared twice in one file also went unflagged; caught at merge time in CI rather than abandoning readable sequential ids
evidence: caught loudly by CI, never silent.

question: Why did spectastic decide to hold its own repository to the strictest standard it offers other projects, and what turned up when it did?
answer: Spectastic's enterprise profile is the standard it holds downstream projects to, but the tool did not hold itself to it: there was no profile marker, so enforce had never certified the repo, which the maintainers call a credibility hole. Mapping the repo against the floor found formatter, linter and coverage genuinely absent, and security and supply-chain covered in substance but invisible to the detector, because the repo uses a bespoke red-team gate and Dependabot while the detector only looks for Semgrep and Renovate. The Dependabot blind spot is a real defect that every downstream project on Dependabot would also hit.
core: it enforced the enterprise floor on others but had never certified itself (a credibility hole); formatter, linter and coverage were missing; the detector missed Dependabot, a defect affecting downstream projects too
evidence: The tool does not hold itself to it
